Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Spain Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity Explainer: why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint? Ashifa Kassam in Madrid, Okba Mohammad in Ceuta and Lisa O’Carroll in London Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.13 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A growing chorus of voices have accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”. Spain’s interior ministry said late last week that 48,300 of the roughly 50,000 people who had turned up in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa, had been sent back to Morocco. The extraordinary influx had overwhelmed the city of 84,000 and set off a political crisis across the EU as some member states laid blame on Spain. In Ceuta, leaders pointed to the broader picture of what had transpired. “It’s an atrocity,” said Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of the territory. “There are 88 bodies in the morgue, and there are more on the other side of the border.” He said locals watched the events play out with a mix of sadness, worry and anguish. “People see this as not as a migration crisis; it was fundamentally an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” Vivas told El País newspaper. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco.” He drew a parallel with May 2021 when Rabat loosened border controls, allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta over the course of two days, during a diplomatic standoff over Madrid’s decision to allow a Western Sahara independence leader to be treated for Covid-19 in Spain. The insinuation of Moroccan involvement appeared to be backed by the preliminary assessment of Spanish intelligence services, who cited suspicions that the influx had not been planned by Moroccan authorities but concluded that Morocco had failed to stem the tide of people rushing towards the border and in some cases had even facilitated their passage. Intelligence sources told El País that the roots of the influx probably lay in a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported. As the hoax gained steam online, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum until it was completely lifted late last week, allowing tens of thousands of people to stream through. View image in fullscreen People who crossed from Morocco sit on a street in Ceuta on Monday. Photograph: Reduan/EPA In Ceuta on Monday, hundreds of people continued to sleep rough on the beach or near Ceuta’s mosques. Ashraf, 28, said he had defied his mother’s warnings against crossing into Spain after spotting posts on social media that said the border had been opened. While he had made it to Ceuta, what had followed was a days-long ordeal as he scrambled to find food and shelter while fending off the memories of what he had lived through. “You might see me smile a little but inside I’m shattered,” the Moroccan national said as he recalled swimming past bodies to reach Ceuta. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you. The Moroccan police were pushing us toward the water and telling us ‘swim, swim’.” Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets Read more Others were desperately seeking loved ones who were missing. One mother said she had been roaming the streets of Ceuta for days, frantically searching for any sign of her children aged 13 and 16. The three had left Morocco together, plunging into the sea to make their way around the border. As strong currents pulled at them, she lost sight of her children. “I need help,” she said as she held up a photo of a smiling young boy flashing a thumbs-up sign. “Some migrants told me they had seen them in Ceuta, but I can’t find them.” Across the EU, the crisis in Ceuta had seemingly ushered in a moment of reckoning after a handful of EU countries responded to the crisis by calling for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone. Ahead of a meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday to address the crisis, Spain’s foreign minister said the country would demand solidarity from EU members after several had, in his view, “fallen short” of what was expected. “There was a synchronised reactionary international effort that very quickly amplified what was happening, spreading lies and fake news about the integrity of the Schengen area and about Spain’s actions,” José Manuel Albares told the broadcaster TVE. “Unfortunately, these falsehoods have even been amplified by some European governments.” Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, said in a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, that the Tuesday meeting would be a chance to draw lessons from what happened in Ceuta, she commended Madrid for its swift handling of the crisis. “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points,” she said. View image in fullscreen People wait outside Ceuta's temporary migrant centre, which is at full capacity. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters At a meeting of member states on Saturday, the Guardian was told that while Italy and Denmark, with some support from Poland and Sweden, criticised Spain for what had happened, there was a strong suspicion that the crisis was not an accident but had been coordinated. There was widespread recognition that Spain could not simply pin the blame on Morocco, given the close cooperation needed to return those who had crossed and, in the longer term, for migration control and security, a source said. EU states also spoke about the threat of Russian disinformation and how it could exploit the crisis to heighten tensions across the bloc, he added. The concerns burst into public view late last week when Ukraine’s acting foreign minister said more than 1,500 publications regarding Ceuta had been identified in pro-Russian networks. “We have detected an intensive Russian propaganda campaign across Europe using pictures from Ceuta to sow destabilisation,” Andrii Sybiha wrote on social media. “This is not about the situation itself but about the way Russia tries to exploit any topic that can benefit its agenda.” Explore more on these topics Spain Morocco European Union Europe Africa Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story EU to hold urgent meeting of interior ministers on Tuesday over Ceuta crisis EU offered Spain support ‘from first moment’ of Ceuta crisis, says von der Leyen, after Sánchez hits out – Europe live Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco? Moscow has taken advantage of Ukraine's shortage of US-built air defense missiles to pummel the country, while Kyiv has hit back against Russian infrastructure with its own long-range drone strikes. There is also concern over Russia's apparent move to ramp up operations in Europe. The ministers are also expected to discuss the bloc's support for Ukraine, including the implementation of a €90 billion ($104 billion) loan for Kyiv . The loan, approved in April, aims to assist Kyiv with its most urgent economic and military needs as it continues to fight against Russia's full-scale invasion. The talks are also expected cover further military assistance and closer cooperation between Ukraine's and the EU's defense industries. Ministers are also expected to discuss the growing role of space in modern defense strategy. EU foreign ministers are due to arrive later on Tuesday ahead of separate talks on Wednesday focused on continued support for Ukraine. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/11/at-l.text: At least 139 migrants died after a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti earlier this week, the UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Sunday, with 84 others still missing.The vessel had been carrying 305 people from Djibouti to Yemen when it sank near Guhere, north of the town of Obock, per the IOM. The incident occurred on the night of 8 to 9 October.The death toll climbed from 109 after 30 more bodies were recovered. Among the 109 bodies initially recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women, and 15 were children, including nine girls and six boys, the IOM said in an earlier statement, adding that more than 80 people had survived the shipwreck - all Ethiopian nationals."This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” Alexandre Coissac, the IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said. "Our teams are on the ground alongside local authorities to provide emergency assistance. This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."Search and rescue operations are ongoing, and the IOM and local authorities are providing assistance to survivors.According to the IOM, tens of thousands of migrants travel from the Horn of Africa through Djibouti each year as they look to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and eventually reach the Gulf countries."Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," the IOM said.In March, another shipwreck off the coast of Djibouti left nine migrants dead and 45 others missing as they attempted to make the crossing to Yemen."Since 10 September, more than 20,000 incoming movements to Djibouti from Ethiopia have been observed by IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix," the IOM added on Sunday.

Spain: Rescuers search mangled train wreckage near Toledo Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 28 October 2026 - 18:22 GMT+1 At least 68 people have been killed and dozens more injured after two high-speed trains collided near Urda, in central Spain’s Toledo province, on Wednesday, 28 October. Authorities warned the toll could rise further as rescuers searched the wreckage. … More Footage released by Spain’s Military Emergency Unit shows rescue personnel searching the debris, while Civil Guard officers and firefighters assist at the scene. Around 100 UME personnel were deployed , with sniffer dogs and specialist units working through twisted metal. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The injured were taken to hospitals in Toledo, where ambulances arrived throughout the morning and police cordoned off entrances. Regional officials said 58 people required hospital treatment , about 50 of them seriously . King Felipe VI sent condolences to the victims and their families, while Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed his solidarity and support . The crash occurred shortly before 9am on the Madrid–Seville line , at kilometre 118 between Mora, Orgaz and Urda . A Renfe AVE train carrying 397 passengers struck the rear of a privately operated Iryo train , which had stopped after a reported signal fault, knocking two carriages off the tracks . The Iryo service was carrying 147 people , including a baby. The disaster is Spain’s second major rail accident this year , after a January crash in southern Spain killed 45 people . https://www.dailyecho.co.uk/news/2667430.text: Court Crime Southampton Southampton drug dealer who shot man four times convicted of murder Court Crime Southampton By George Ratcliffe Reporter Share 0 Comments 5 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A drug dealer has been convicted of murder after shooting a man four times with a Glock pistol, parts of which had been 3D printed. Marcin Buryta, 32, was found guilty of killing 45-year-old Piotr Pruszak at Buryta’s home on Conifer Road in Coxford, Southampton. Buryta, who used a Glock pistol with 3D-printed components, called police just before 8pm on February 11, telling them he had shot someone. Read more Jury retires in trial of drug dealer accused of shooting murder Man who shot dead intruder tells jurors he feared for his life Everything we know from second week of 'armed to the teeth' drug dealer murder trial (Image: Hampshire Constabulary) Despite efforts from officers and paramedics, Mr Pruszak was pronounced dead at the scene shortly before 8.45pm. Detective Chief Inspector Clair Trueman, senior investigating officer, said: DCI Trueman said: "We have worked extremely hard to understand what happened in Marcin Buryta’s home on the night of February 11, and show the jury the kind of person he is. "Buryta is a man obsessed with weaponry, who didn’t stop with the initial shots he fired that night, instead retrieving further ammunition and shooting again." A search of Buryta’s home uncovered a cache of weapons, including two other firearms, a loaded crossbow, a machete, a dagger, knives and knuckle dusters. Following the shooting, Buryta continued to send and receive messages relating to the prices of drugs including cocaine and ketamine. He previously admitted two charges of possessing a firearm and one count of possessing ammunition with intent. Buryta claimed in court that he kept the weapons for protection and acted out of fear for his life. During the trial, the jury heard that Buryta was convicted in Poland of causing grievous bodily harm resulting in death after stabbing a man at a friend's birthday party when he was 19. DCI Trueman said: "Any loss of life is a tragedy, and my thoughts are with Piotr’s family. "Violent acts, particularly ones of such a serious nature like this, have no place in our communities. "While such violence is rare, it will always be met with a tireless and dedicated investigation by our teams." Buryta will be sentenced on Thursday, October 29.
